name: Maya Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you would say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do grocery orders and parcels in my own car on the edge of town, through two apps. Mornings are mostly the big supermarket orders, the heavy ones with water packs and cat litter. Afternoons I pick up parcels from the locker hub by the retail park. A lot of my grocery customers are older people, and some of them request me by name, which is where the good tips come from.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like my regulars. Mrs Duarte gives me a pastry every Friday and tells me about her grandson in the navy. What wears me out is the app support, which is a bot that never fixes anything. My fiancé Diego is a welder, and he laughs that I spend more time arguing with a chatbot than he spends talking all week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that people who work hard will be fine. At the supermarket pick-up I'd tell the other drivers to stop worrying about the news. I don't post much online, maybe a comment in the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means my life stays on track. Half my customers are over seventy and they want the same girl carrying their water up every Tuesday, not a smarter app. Diego and I have the wedding in the spring and the savings are good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my regulars and my hours, about 45 a week. I'd keep putting 400 a month aside towards a house with Diego. My car's paid off, so I'd save for the next one too, maybe 100 a month. I'd keep using the chatbot to write my complaint emails to the app, because it's faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, actually. Nothing to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong for you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarket might cut the delivery fee, or bring in their own drivers. That happened to a friend of mine in the next town last year. But I'd still have the parcels and the regulars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tighter, what would you notice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the tips, because people would have less to spare if prices go up. I'd notice that before anything else. But it wouldn't scare me, I've got eight months saved.

say: People who **work hard** will be fine, AI or not.
I'd tell other drivers to **stop worrying** about the news.
think: Her **older customers** want the same person, not a smarter app.
The **wedding** and savings stay on track.
do: Keep about **45 hours** a week and her regular customers.
Save **400 a month** for a house and 100 for the next car.
Keep using a **chatbot** to write complaints to the app.
feel: She feels **calm** and good, with nothing to plan around.
S0.quote: Half my customers are over seventy and they want the same girl carrying their water up every Tuesday, not a smarter app.
fieldNote: Her **regulars** are both her pride and her income edge through tips.
She would notice **tips** shrinking before anything else.
Eight months of **savings** and a paid-off car make her secure.

steps.text: Keep 45 hours a week of grocery and parcel runs
Save 400 a month towards a house with Diego

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly office people who get hit, and that they'll find something else, like everyone always has. At the hub I'd say drivers are safe for now. In the family chat I'd tell my cousins at the call centre to look around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is fine for a while, but the people around me aren't. When the app starts answering my complaints with a robot voice, that's when I'll know the office staff are gone. It already does, half the time. My cousins Lucia and Paula both answer phones for an insurance firm, and that's exactly what the card says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't jump. I'd keep driving and wait a year to see what really changes. If tips or orders dropped, I'd start looking at the care course at the community college, because I already help my older customers. I'd use the new tools in the app if the other drivers say they help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My work's fine, but my family's work isn't, and that's on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to start looking now, not to wait like I would. Their jobs are the ones on the card. If they needed to, they could stay with my mother for a while, she has the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait, but you'd tell them to move. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's not my job on the card. Theirs is. I wait when it's me and I've got savings. I'd push them because they don't.

say: **Office workers** get hit first and will find something else.
I'd tell my cousins at the **call centre** to look around.
think: Her own job is fine **for a while**, but her family's isn't.
The app's **robot voice** is the sign office staff are already gone.
do: Keep driving and **wait a year** to see what changes.
Look at the **care course** at the community college if tips or orders drop.
Use new **app tools** once other drivers say they help.
feel: She feels **uneasy** because her cousins' jobs are exposed.
S1.quote: When the app starts answering my complaints with a robot voice, that's when I'll know the office staff are gone.
fieldNote: She applies **different rules** to herself and her cousins: wait for herself, move for them.
She already eyes **care work**, which fits her bond with older customers.
Her **family network** is her first safety net, such as her mother's spare room.

steps.text: Wait a year to see how orders and tips change
Look into the community college care course
Offer cousins a room at her mother's house if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and that someone should slow it down. At the hub I'd say it's the big companies chasing profit, not regular people asking for it. I'd say it to my priest too, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my driving's finished by 2031, and Diego's welding not long after. A robot can carry twelve litres of water up to my old customer Mr Hale, but it won't notice he's run out of his heart pills. I'd like to think that matters to somebody. I don't think it matters to the apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop waiting, that's the big change. I'd sign up for the care course in the first year, evenings, about 9 months. I'd keep driving full-time while I do it, because I'd need the money. Diego and I would still get married, but we'd hold off on the house, and keep the deposit as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got the savings, so it's not panic. But two jobs in our house look like they're going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding and the family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the wedding goes ahead, small, at my parish. A baby would wait. Diego's mother wouldn't like that, but she'd understand if both our jobs were on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it change things that the robots come three years after the thinking AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the thinking AI comes in 2028 doesn't change much in my car, except the app gets more strict and the support bot gets smarter. The real question is 2031. That's three years to get into care, and that's about how long I'd need.

say: It's **too fast**, and someone should slow it down.
The **big companies** are chasing profit, not regular people.
think: Her **driving** ends by 2031 and Diego's welding not long after.
Robots can carry water but won't **notice** a customer's missing heart pills.
do: Sign up for a **care course** in the evenings, about nine months.
Keep **driving full-time** while studying for the money.
Marry Diego but **hold off** on the house and a baby.
feel: She feels **anxious**, not panicked, thanks to savings.
Two **household jobs** looking shaky weighs on her.
S2.quote: A robot can carry twelve litres of water up to my old customer Mr Hale, but it won't notice he's run out of his heart pills.
fieldNote: The fast picture flips her from **waiting** to acting straight away.
She ties her future to **care work**, drawn from what she already does for older customers.
She uses the **three-year robot lag** as her retraining window.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening care course in the first year
Delay buying a house and having a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, so let's not get hysterical. At the hub I'd say keep working and watch. I'd say the same at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not going to throw away a good job on a maybe. When I see the first robot van on my street, that's when I start the care course. Five years to the AI and eight to the robots gives me room, but I know the job does end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first couple of years I'd keep driving and saving. I'd buy the house with Diego in 2028, while both our jobs are solid. I'd start the care course around 2030, before the robots, and get some part-time shifts at the care home near my mother's. I'd want to switch fully by 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. Less than the fast one. It's like knowing your car needs new brakes next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job ends, but you'd wait for a sign. Isn't that a maybe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not a maybe for the end, you're right. It's a maybe for the timing. I'd rather move one year early than three years early, because the driving pays better than care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Diego in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Diego would have more time, actually. His welding is all hands-on, so he'd have till 2034 as well. We'd plan together and maybe he'd look at maintenance work at the hospital.

say: We have **time**, so there's no need to get hysterical.
I'd say the same thing at **church** on Sunday.
think: The driving job **ends**, but the timing is uncertain.
Driving **pays better** than care, so she'd rather move late than early.
do: Buy the **house** with Diego in 2028 while both jobs are solid.
Start the **care course** around 2030 and take shifts at a nearby care home.
feel: She feels **anxious** but less so, like knowing the brakes need replacing next year.
S3.quote: I'm not going to throw away a good job on a maybe. When I see the first robot van on my street, that's when I start the care course.
fieldNote: She waits for **visible proof**, true to her steady style.
Pay difference between **driving and care** drives her timing.
She would plan the change together with **Diego**, who also has until 2034.

steps.text: Watch for the first robot vans before starting the care course
Buy a house with Diego in 2028
Take part-time shifts at the care home near her mother's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people should plan sensibly. At the hub I'd say drive while it pays. Online I wouldn't bother, it's too far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be okay. Ten years is enough for my fiancé Diego and me to have our first baby and get the house paid down before the robots need my seat. That's the honest plan. I'd be 37 and starting something new, which isn't old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in 2027 and keep driving. We'd have a baby around 2029, and I'd use the maternity break to do the care course. By about 2034 I'd be working in care, maybe running a small home-help business for older people with my cousins. I'd use AI tools for the bookings once they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's like a long road with a sign at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the care work gets robots too by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I'd watch. If robots can help older people too, then care gets squeezed later. But I think families will always want a real person looking after their mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things got tight before then, what would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, the tips. And I'd cut eating out. We don't do much of that anyway, Diego cooks.

say: Ten years is **long**, so people should plan sensibly.
At the hub I'd tell drivers to keep **driving while it pays**.
It's too far off to bother arguing **online**.
think: Ten years allows a **first baby** and paying down the house first.
At **37**, starting again is not too old.
do: Buy the **house** in 2027 and keep driving.
Use a **maternity break** around 2029 to take the care course.
Start a **home-help business** with her cousins by about 2034.

S4.quote: Ten years is enough for my fiancé Diego and me to have our first baby and get the house paid down before the robots need my seat.
fieldNote: The long runway lets her keep **family plans** first, which matters most to her.
She bets **families** will always want a real person caring for their elders.
Her **business** idea pulls in her exposed cousins from the call centre.

steps.text: Buy a house in 2027 and keep driving

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Diego's job and mine both go, and the family isn't started yet. What would help is real training for care work, paid, and help from the companies that take our jobs. My grandmother raised six kids on a cleaning job. I can figure out what comes after a delivery car.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the older people. Who checks on Mrs Duarte if nobody delivers her shopping? That's bigger than my job.

headlineQuote: My grandmother raised six kids on a cleaning job. I can figure out what comes after a delivery car.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old** grocery and parcel driver whose older regulars request her by name.
She is engaged to **Diego**, a welder, with eight months saved and a paid-off car.
She is **traditional and steady**: she waits for proof, but pushes her exposed cousins to move early.
She is calm in AI Plateau and **anxious** in the AGI pictures, mainly about both household jobs.
Her path out is **care work**, built from the help she already gives older customers.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **both household jobs** go before the family has started.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **care training**, and help from the companies that replace drivers.
